surface_summary: Reginald Templeton is found murdered on his yacht at Marsh Quay. Suspicion falls on several men including an artist lodger, a diamond dealer, and a retired cigar merchant, with clues such as a cigar band and a walking-stick complicating the investigation.
accepted_facts: Templeton was murdered on his yacht sometime around midnight.
A cigar band found at the scene was initially thought to implicate the artist Grayson.
A walking-stick was found in the dinghy, suggesting the murderer left it behind.
Norwood was the coroner and a respected lawyer with financial troubles.
inferred_conclusions: The artist Grayson was the murderer due to the cigar band evidence.
Isaac Moss fled because he was guilty of the murder.
The cigar band found was unique and exclusive to Canon Fittleworth’s cigars.
mechanism_description: Norwood, fearing exposure for his embezzlement, arranged a meeting with Templeton under the pretense of settling a blackmail demand. He accompanied Templeton back to the yacht, where he murdered him with a dagger. Norwood staged the scene by changing the cigar band and planting a dummy walking-stick to mislead the investigation.
delivery_path: Norwood sent his domestics to a public event to ensure privacy.
He met Templeton in Frattenbury and walked back with him to Marsh Quay.
Norwood boarded the yacht with Templeton using the dinghy.
He killed Templeton with a dagger during the meeting on the yacht.
Norwood rifled Templeton’s pockets and took papers to cover his tracks.
He returned to shore in the dinghy, then used a canoe to return the dinghy to the yacht.
Norwood altered the cigar band at the inquest to deflect suspicion.
outcome_result: Francis Norwood is arrested for the murder of Reginald Templeton and commits suicide in custody.

false_assumption.statement: The cigar band found at the scene uniquely identified the artist Grayson as the murderer.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: The cigar band was found at the crime scene and matched the brand smoked by Grayson, linking him to the yacht at the time of the murder. The presence of multiple bands of the same brand in the grate reinforced this belief.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: The cigar band was switched during the inquest by the coroner to implicate Grayson falsely. The actual murderer, Norwood, possessed the same brand and manipulated the evidence to mislead investigators.

supporting_points: Cigar bands matching his cigars were found at the crime scene.
He left the inn suddenly early on the morning the murder was discovered.
He had a motive due to a family feud with Templeton.
He could not provide a full alibi for the night.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The cigar band evidence was tampered with by the coroner, and Grayson was verified to have been at a different location overnight.

red_herrings.description: Isaac Moss fled suddenly after the murder and was found with diamonds linked to Templeton.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: Moss was frightened of being suspected and had legitimate business with Templeton involving diamonds; he was at a hotel during the murder.

red_herrings.description: The cigar band found at the scene was thought to be unique and incriminating.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: The cigar band was switched during the inquest by the coroner to implicate Grayson falsely; the brand was common among several people.

closed_circle.rationale: The investigation narrowed down to four main suspects with access and motives, all local or connected to Marsh Quay, with no outsiders involved.

Midnight to 1 am - estimated time of murder
Sunday early morning - discovery of body
time_windows: Saturday night - inquest and public house closing time
Sunday morning - arrival of police and witnesses

inference_path.correction: The stick was a dummy planted to mislead
inference_path.effect: Indicates murderer left the stick deliberately

Comparison of stick ferrule with known walking-sticks

inference_path.observation: Cigar band found at crime scene matched Grayson’s cigars
inference_path.correction: Band was switched during inquest by coroner
inference_path.effect: Exonerates Grayson from suspicion based on cigar evidence
required_evidence: Testimony of Canon Fittleworth rejecting band as his own
Witness accounts of band passing through jury hands

inference_path.observation: Isaac Moss fled suddenly after murder
inference_path.correction: Moss fled out of fear, not guilt
inference_path.effect: Moss is innocent despite suspicious behavior
required_evidence: Hotel registration and witness statements confirming Moss’s presence
Receipt and diamonds accounted for by Moss

inference_path.observation: Norwood had financial troubles and access to the scene
inference_path.correction: Norwood’s motive was to prevent blackmail exposure
required_evidence: Norwood’s ownership of walking-stick matching dummy
Norwood’s presence near yacht at time of murder

inference_path.observation: Blotting-pad letter mentioning 'Ezra Grice’s confession & proof'
inference_path.correction: Letter implicates Norwood’s past crime and blackmail
inference_path.effect: Connects Norwood to motive for murder
required_evidence: Testimony of Ezra Grice about Norwood’s embezzlement

inference_path.observation: Norwood’s alibi challenged by witness Merrifield
inference_path.correction: Merrifield confirms Norwood’s presence at dinner until 1:30 am
inference_path.effect: Narrows time window for murder and confirms Norwood’s opportunity
required_evidence: Time of death estimated by doctor

inference_path.observation: Norwood changed cigar band at inquest
inference_path.correction: This was an attempt to mislead investigation
required_evidence: Discovery of original band in Norwood’s possession

discriminating_test.design: Detective Colson planted the original walking-stick in the dinghy and watched to see if the suspect would attempt to retrieve it. The suspect’s behavior in attempting to recover the stick would confirm his guilt.
discriminating_test.knowledge_revealed: The test revealed that Norwood was the only one who tried to recover the walking-stick, confirming his involvement.
discriminating_test.pass_condition: The suspect must be observed attempting to retrieve the planted walking-stick from the dinghy.

fair_play_explanation: The reader is given all necessary clues including the cigar band, walking-stick, witness testimonies, and the blotting-pad letter. The detective’s reasoning is transparent and the false leads are clearly marked. The key to the solution lies in recognizing the tampering of the cigar band and the significance of the walking-stick, both of which are presented openly. The motive of blackmail and Norwood’s financial troubles are also revealed early enough for the reader to deduce the culprit.
